title: Incense
hook: let my prayer rise like incense (Psalm 141:2)

segments.voice: Yesterday, colors of the year: purple, white, red and green, a calendar you can see. Your line was time has colors. What color did you choose for the season you're in? Day one thousand three hundred sixty.

The smell arrives first. Sweet and sharp, resin and wood smoke, and it reaches the back of the church before the procession does. Then the sound: a small chain clinking. A priest comes up the aisle swinging a metal censer, and with every swing a gray ribbon of smoke curls out, hangs in the light from a high window, and slowly climbs. He turns and swings it toward the icons, toward the altar, and then toward the people, who bow as it passes. By the end of the service the smoke has drifted up into the roof, and the smell is in everyone's coats. Today: incense.

Incense is a part of worship you can watch going up. And more than one passage in the Bible ties that rising smoke to prayer. Start with the psalm. "Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense; and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice." The psalmist wants their prayer to do what the smoke does: rise, and be noticed. Next, the temple. At the start of Luke's Gospel, a priest named Zechariah is chosen by lot to go into the temple and burn incense. And Luke adds a detail: "And the whole multitude of the people were praying without at the time of incense." Inside, smoke. Outside, prayer. The same hour, as if they were one act. Then, a gift. When the wise men find the child Jesus, they open their treasures: "gold, and frankincense, and myrrh." Frankincense is incense, brought by travelers from the east to be given away. Last, heaven itself. In the book of Revelation, an angel stands at the altar with a golden censer, "And the smoke of the incense, which came with the prayers of the saints, ascended up before God out of the angel's hand." In that picture, the prayers rise all the way to God. Orthodox and Catholic Christians use incense in worship, and so do some Anglican and Lutheran churches. Other Christians pray without it, and keep to the psalm's thought without the smoke. In the psalm's picture, a prayer isn't meant to stay on the ground. It rises.
screen: `LET MY PRAYER BE SET FORTH AS INCENSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light incense, or smell a spice. If you have incense and it's safe to light, light it, set it down, and watch the smoke climb. If not, open a jar from the kitchen, cinnamon, cloves, a bay leaf, and breathe it in slowly. Settle, and let the scent fill one breath, then another. Watch the smoke rise, or picture your breath rising. If you pray, you can say the psalm: let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense. Or simply follow the scent, breath by breath. The bell holds the time.
screen: `LET MY PRAYER BE SET FORTH BEFORE THEE AS INCENSE.`

segments.voice: Incense. Fragrant smoke burned in worship, which the Bible links to prayer: you can watch it rise.
Your line: prayer rises. Today, when you notice steam from a cup or smoke from a chimney, let it carry one hope of yours upward. Day one thousand three hundred sixty.

howItsDone: In Orthodox and Catholic worship, and in some Anglican and Lutheran churches, a priest or deacon swings a censer toward the altar, the icons or the gospel book, and the people; other churches pray without incense.

original.note: Hebrew: incense, the word in Psalm 141:2, "let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense."

trapdoor: what you thought: incense is there to make the church smell nice.
what it means: smoke that rises the way a prayer hopes to, a prayer you can watch.
what a scholar hears: Luke 1:10, the whole multitude praying outside "at the time of incense": smoke and prayer kept to the same hour.

notes: Hook's censing order (icons, altar, people) is a general description, not a rubric; confirm for Orthodox and Catholic use.
'Frankincense is incense, carried a long way to be given away': the distance is inferred from the wise men coming 'from the east' (Matthew 2:1); confirm acceptable.
Use of incense attributed to Orthodox, Catholic and some Anglican and Lutheran churches; confirm.
Hebrew qetoret in Psalm 141:2; confirm pointing and transliteration.
Practice includes a safety condition for lighting incense; a spice is offered as an alternative.

Editor: removed the superlative 'the one part of worship'; 'carried a long way' now follows Matthew 2:1 ('from the east'); dropped the interpretive 'ordinary believers'; closing image framed as the psalm's, not the narrator's.
